summary: Documents the object identifiers assigned in the arc set aside for the Long-Term Archive and Notary Services working group, and sets IANA allocation policies for future assignments in that arc. This is administrative bookkeeping rather than a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a list of the numbered name tags one working group handed out, plus rules for giving new ones.

subtitle: A bookkeeping record of the object identifiers the LTANS working group handed out, and the rules for adding more.

tldr.problem: The LTANS working group had an object identifier arc set aside, and several documents used values in it without a single record of what was assigned or how new values would be handed out.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the three subordinate arcs and the identifiers assigned in each, and has IANA create registry tables for them, with Expert Review for updates.
tldr.outcome: One place records the module identifiers, CMS content types and the obsolete encryption method identifier. Future values must be closely tied to the LTANS work.

today: RFC 7036 is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the record of what was assigned in the LTANS arc and how future values are allocated.

sections.title: The LTANS Identifier Arc
sections.content:
When the Long-Term Archive and Notary Services (LTANS) working group was chartered, an object identifier arc was set aside for it. These identifiers are mainly used with Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1). The arc is id-ltans, which is 1.3.6.1.5.5.11.

The memo describes the identifiers that were assigned and sets IANA allocation policies for future assignments. It is a record, not a protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A working group got its own street of numbered addresses. This memo writes down which houses on the street are taken.

sections.title: Subordinate Arcs and What They Hold
sections.content:
Three subordinate arcs were used: id-mod (value 0) for ASN.1 module identifiers, id-ct (value 1) for Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) content types, and id-em (value 2) for Evidence Record Syntax (ERS) encryption methods.

Module identifiers cover the ERS modules of RFC 4998, the Long-term Archive Protocol (LTAP) modules, the SCVP long-term evidence record conventions of RFC 5276, and the Data Structure for the Security Suitability of Cryptographic Algorithms (DSSC) of RFC 5698. Where a protocol has two modules, they define the same syntax in the 1988 and the 1997 ASN.1 forms. LTAP was never published as an RFC, but its identifiers were assigned to help implementation.

For content types, an Evidence Record type was reserved but no specification points to it. RFC 5698 specifies three (id-ct-dssc-asn1, id-ct-dssc-xml and id-ct-dssc-tbsPolicy), and LTAP defines two, a request and a response.

One encryption method identifier, id-em-enveloped-data, was assigned, but it is obsolete and should not be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The street has three side streets: one for document formats, one for kinds of message, and one for a way of scrambling that is no longer used.

sections.title: IANA Tables and Allocation Policy
sections.content:
IANA updated one registry table and created four more within the SMI Security Codes registry: one for the LTANS arc itself, and one each for module identifiers, CMS content types and ERS encryption methods. The existing entry for Long-Term Archive and Notary Services (decimal value 11) now points to this document.

Updates to the four new tables require Expert Review as defined in RFC 5226. The Designated Expert is expected to make sure new values are strongly related to the LTANS working group's work. Identifiers for other purposes should not be assigned in this arc.
sections.plainLanguage: To add a new name tag you need an expert to agree, and the tag must be about this working group's own work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo populates an IANA registry and raises no new security considerations. The protocols that specify these values carry the security considerations for their usage.
sections.plainLanguage: A list of name tags does not add any new dangers. The programs that use the tags handle the safety questions.
